key_insight: Large language models can generate their own replay data—sampling from their learned distribution—to nearly eliminate forgetting during continued training; forgetting still appears when the model runs out of representational/optimization capacity.
problem_solved: Mitigates catastrophic forgetting in continual learning without storing real exemplars, addressing data-storage, privacy, and practicality constraints of traditional replay methods.
method: Use the model to self-sample examples from its training distribution and include these synthetic examples as replay data during subsequent task training.
Empirically compare self-generated replay to stored-exemplar replay and no-replay baselines to quantify forgetting and downstream performance.
Analyze how model capacity and optimization dynamics limit the effectiveness of self-generated replay, identifying regimes where forgetting persists.
impact: Enables practical, storage- and privacy-friendly continual learning for language models by replacing exemplar buffers with self-generated replay, while highlighting that capacity/optimization constraints must be managed to fully avoid forgetting.
visual_elements: Timeline diagram contrasting training with no replay, stored-exemplar replay, and self-generated replay, annotated with accuracy drops
Line chart of forgetting magnitude vs model capacity showing near-zero forgetting until a capacity threshold
Flowchart of the self-replay loop: sample → filter/weight → mix with new-task data → continue training
Icon set comparing storage-heavy replay (disk icon) vs self-replay (generation/robot icon) plus a lock for privacy
paper_title: Forgetting in Language Models: Capacity, Optimization, and Self-Generated Replay
paper_authors: Martin Marek, Dongkyu Cho, Shikai Qiu, Rumi Chunara, Pavel Izmailov
